note.explanation: Taxonomic ranks arrange organisms in levels, from the broadest group, domain, to the most specific group, species. Each level is divided into smaller, related groups.
examples: In the table in your textbook, a human belongs to the domain Eukarya and the species Homo sapiens.
For plants and fungi, the rank corresponding to phylum is called division.
note.checkAnswer: Domain, kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus, species.
note.simple: Think of classification as sorting organisms into groups that get smaller and more specific at each step.
note.checkQuestion: Name the highest and lowest taxonomic ranks.
note.title: Taxonomic ranks: broad groups to specific groups
steps: Start with the broadest rank: domain.
Move down through kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family and genus.
Finish with species, the lowest rank.
note.answer: The highest rank is domain; the lowest rank is species.

mcqs.stem: Which taxonomic rank is the broadest?
rationales: Species is the lowest taxonomic rank, not the broadest.
Family is below order and is much narrower than domain.
Domain is the highest and broadest taxonomic rank.
Genus is above species but below family.

options: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, domain, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
Domain, phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom, domain
mcqs.stem: Which list shows the taxonomic ranks in order from broadest to most specific?
rationales: This gives the ranks in the correct descending order.
Domain comes before kingdom, and phylum comes before class; this list reverses those relationships.
Kingdom comes before phylum, and order comes before family; this list reverses both relationships.
This is the order from most specific to broadest, not broadest to most specific.

mcqs.stem: Which rank is the lowest level of classification?
rationales: Kingdom is high in the hierarchy and is not the lowest rank.
Order is above family, genus and species.
Species is defined as the lowest level of classification.
Class is above order, family, genus and species.

mcqs.stem: A family is divided into related groups called:
rationales: A family is divided into related genera; genus is singular and genera is plural.
Families are themselves subdivisions of orders, so this is not the rank below family.
Phylum is a much broader rank than family.
Kingdom is broader still and is not the rank below family.

mcqs.stem: Each class is further divided into related:
rationales: Phylum is above class in the hierarchy.
Each class is further divided into related orders.
Family is below order, not directly below class.
Class is the rank named in the question, not the rank into which it is divided.

mcqs.stem: Which term is used in place of phylum for plants and fungi?
rationales: Phylum is the general term, but the textbook gives a different term for plants and fungi.
Division is the term used for plants and fungi in place of phylum.
Kingdom is a separate, higher taxonomic rank.
Order is a lower rank than class and is not another name for phylum.

options: It is divided directly into species.
It is another name for family.
mcqs.stem: Which statement about species agrees with the textbook definition?
rationales: The highest rank is domain, not species.
Species is the lowest level of classification.
Genus is the rank directly above species; the textbook does not say a rank is divided directly into species.
Species and family are different taxonomic ranks.

options: A scientist who added domain in 1977
The botanist who classified only animals
A botanist who suggested just three ranks
mcqs.stem: Who devised the Linnaean system of taxonomic ranks in 1735?
rationales: Carl Linnaeus devised the Linnaean system in 1735.
The textbook says domain was added to the system in 1977, not that this person devised it.
The textbook identifies Linnaeus as a Swedish botanist and does not say he classified only animals.
Linnaeus suggested seven ranks, not just three.

written.text: Describe the Linnaean system of classification in detail, stating the seven taxonomic ranks and their relationships.
written.finalAnswer: The Linnaean system arranges organisms into related groups in a hierarchy. The seven ranks, from broadest to most specific, are kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus and species. Each kingdom is subdivided into phyla or divisions; each phylum or division into classes; each class into orders; each order into families; each family into genera; and species is the lowest level. Domain was added as the highest rank in 1977.

written.text: How might placing an organism in the incorrect taxonomic group affect conservation or scientific studies?
written.finalAnswer: Incorrect classification can cause scientists to misunderstand an organism's relationships to other organisms. This may lead to unsuitable conservation decisions and make scientific information or comparisons about the organism unreliable.

written.text: Imagine you discover a new organism. What steps would you take to classify and name it according to the principles of binomial nomenclature?
written.finalAnswer: I would study the organism's characteristics and compare them with known organisms to place it in the correct taxonomic groups. I would then identify its genus and distinguish it as a new species. I would give it a two-part scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name, using the correct scientific-name format.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask you to list the seven Linnaean ranks. Write them in order from kingdom to species.
A question may ask for the three domains. Learn the exact names: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

For full marks, include that domain is the highest rank and species is the lowest level of classification.
When classifying an organism, label each rank clearly and keep the sequence from domain down to species.

explain.title: Ranks are levels of classification
explain.body: The groups into which organisms are classified are known as taxonomic ranks or taxa (singular “taxon”). The ranks form a hierarchy: each step down groups organisms more specifically.

explain.title: The Linnaean ranks
explain.body: Linnaeus suggested seven taxonomic ranks: kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus and species. Domain was added to this system in 1977 and is the highest rank.

explain.title: How the groups fit together
explain.body: A kingdom is divided into phyla or divisions; these are divided into classes, then orders, families and genera. Species is the lowest level of classification.

explain.title: Species
explain.body: It is the lowest level of classification. A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile (capable of reproduction) offspring.

explain.title: Use the plant term correctly
explain.body: For plants and fungi, use division in place of phylum. The other ranks keep the same order.

mistakes: Putting species at the top of the hierarchy; it is the lowest rank.
Leaving out genus or family when listing the ranks.
Reversing the order of the ranks; write from broadest to most specific unless the question asks otherwise.
Forgetting that domain was added in 1977 and is higher than kingdom.
Using phylum instead of division when describing the rank for plants and fungi.
